st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source accepts that average GenAI task gains are uneven and do not by themselves establish broad productivity or skill growth. It materially extends the cluster by identifying AI Interaction Competence—especially eliciting, filtering and verifying outputs—as a predictor of gains, and by providing experimental evidence that conceptual scaffolding and training can reduce performance dispersion without lowering mean performance.
qs: Improvements were not predicted by GPA or prior knowledge, but                                               by AI Interaction Competence (AIC) — the ability to elicit, filter, and verify model outputs.

Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source directly substantiates the cluster’s conditional-distribution proposition: GenAI raised average performance but widened novice dispersion, while AI Interaction Competence determined who benefited. It also materially develops the proposition by showing that structured scaffolding can reduce unequal outcomes, whereas access or additional exposure alone is insufficient.
qs: However, dispersion among novices increased by roughly 47% in standard deviation—more than doubling the variance.
High-AIC                                               participants realized outsized gains; low-AIC participants saw limited or even negative marginal returns.

st.t: Skill gaps: Assisted equality can hide learning divides
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between average AI-assisted gains and unequal underlying capabilities, and materially develops it by identifying AI Interaction Competence as a new axis of advantage. It also provides suggestive evidence that conceptual scaffolding may reduce this divide, while acknowledging limits from attrition, measurement inconsistency and the student setting.
qs: Taken together, these results indicate that generative AI compressed in- equality along conventional academic lines (GPA, prior knowledge) but expanded it along a novel dimension: the ability to interact effectively with AI.

Variance in post-intervention exam scores was lower among scaffolded novices (SD = .14) compared to unguided novices (SD = .22), consistent with the view that scaffolding reduces inequality by leveling the floor.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that GenAI gains depend on user expertise, verification and workflow design, and materially extends it with randomized micro-evidence that AI Interaction Competence moderates performance and that lightweight scaffolding can reduce outcome variance. Its student sample, attrition bias and weakly significant scaffold interaction limit direct generalization to legal work.
qs: Unlike GPA or pre-intervention exam score, which showed no meaningful interaction with treatment, AIC emerged as the decisive moderator of outcomes.

Our study complements this literature by providing controlled, causal micro-evidence: it isolates how differences in AIC levels shape productivity outcomes and demonstrates that lightweight process interventions—conceptual scaffolding and training—reduce variance without lowering mean performance.

st.t: AI learning: Interaction skill shapes novice gains
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it reports higher short-term scores with LLM access while finding that novice gains depend on AI interaction competence rather than novice status alone. It also acknowledges attrition and setting limitations and treats structured guidance as promising rather than proof of persistent or general workplace gains.
qs: For ease of interpretation, we rescaled the pre-intervention exam score which yielded a positive coefficient: novice learners (i.e., those with low prior knowledge) benefited more from LLM-assisted study, but only if they had high AIC levels.
This pattern not only biased final outcomes in favor of the LLM group but also illustrates how technology availability can shape engagement itself.

kp.k: Student experiment models early-career knowledge work
kp.d: Anand and Idan report a randomized experiment involving 179 Texas A&M University students, predominantly engineering undergraduates, studying LLMs. Participants were assigned traditional resources excluding LLMs or only free ChatGPT, with a minimum three hours daily for three consecutive days. Novices, defined as answering fewer than eight of 15 baseline questions correctly, received additional randomized process variants. The authors treat this controlled learning environment as an analogy for early-career knowledge work, not direct evidence about lawyers or workplace production.
qs: The intervention was conducted at Texas A&M University with a total of 179 participants.
Participants were instructed to dedicate a minimum of 3 hours per day for 3 consecutive days to self-study.
The primary outcome is individual task performance (a proxy for knowledge-work productivity).

kp.k: LLM access improved average examination performance
kp.d: Mean normalized post-intervention scores were .56 (SD .26) with LLM access versus .48 (SD .23) with traditional resources. An OLS treatment coefficient remained positive and significant at p < 0.05 after controlling for baseline score, GPA, gender and study preferences. The discussion describes this as an approximate 17% productivity lift; the measured outcome was examination performance after self-study, rather than directly observed professional productivity.
qs: The average post-intervention exam score among LLM participants was M = .56, SD = .26, compared to M = .48, SD = .23 in the baseline group.
The treatment coefficient remained positive and statistically significant (p < 0.05).
GenAI access translated into an approximate 17% productivity lift

kp.k: Differential attrition complicates interpretation of performance advantages
kp.d: Twenty baseline participants withdrew before the final examination versus nine LLM participants; the authors report an association between baseline assignment and attrition at p < 0.01. All performance analyses used completers. The authors interpret dropout as revealed preference for LLM access and acknowledge bias favoring the LLM group, although baseline participants most commonly cited illness or scheduling conflicts. Resource preferences were LLMs 69%, YouTube 67%, lectures 64% and textbooks 40%.
qs: Overall, 20 participants in the baseline group withdrew before the post-intervention exam, compared to only 9 in the LLM group.
Baseline participants most commonly cited illness or scheduling conflicts
This pattern not only biased final outcomes in favor of the LLM group but also illustrates how technology availability can shape engagement itself.
All analyses use the completer sample (post-intervention exam scores available)

kp.k: Interaction competence is the proposed complementary human capability
kp.d: The authors define AI Interaction Competence (AIC) as practical prompting, filtering, verification and iterative refinement skills that translate AI access into useful performance. Their mechanism is human augmentation: users must direct probabilistic outputs, check accuracy, bias and relevance, and combine machine suggestions with judgment. They argue that tool availability alone cannot ensure consistent benefits because these complementary skills are unevenly distributed and rarely taught.
qs: AIC is defined as the set of practical skills and habits that enable an individual to use generative AI systems effectively and reliably in their work.
Filter and verify generative AI’s outputs for accuracy, bias, and relevance rather than accepting them at face value.
Iterate interactively, refining inputs and combining human judgment with machine suggestions to improve quality and efficiency.

kp.k: AIC moderated gains where academic markers did not
kp.d: The GPA–treatment interaction was statistically insignificant (p = 0.59), as was the prior-knowledge interaction (p = 0.2). The authors report a positive Treatment × AIC interaction (p < 0.05), interpreting this as a new axis of performance inequality rather than reinforcement of conventional academic hierarchies. A significant three-way interaction among treatment, baseline score and AIC (p < 0.05) indicated larger benefits for novices conditional on high AIC. The abstract additionally asserts limited or negative marginal returns among low-AIC participants.
qs: The interaction between GPA and treatment assignment was small and statistically insignificant (p = 0.59).
pre-intervention exam scores, which measure prior topic-specific knowledge, did not significantly interact with treatment status (p = 0.2).
In interaction analysis, the coefficient on the (Treatment × AIC) term was positive and significant (p < 0.05).
novice learners (i.e., those with low prior knowledge) benefited more from LLM-assisted study, but only if they had high AIC levels.

kp.k: Calibration findings accompany inconsistent descriptions of AIC measurement
kp.d: The paper reports self-assessment correlations with performance of ρ = .71 for general ML knowledge and ρ = .6 for LLM-specific knowledge, both p < .01, and an AIC association of ρ = .46, p < .05. Its measurement descriptions differ: the survey section lists self-assessed AIC, whereas the results say AIC was neither self-assessed nor tested in the baseline examination and instead inferred behaviorally. The authors' substantive conclusion is that conventional knowledge assessments do not identify the capability driving heterogeneous AI benefits.
qs: Self-assessed knowledge of LLM Interaction Competence (AIC)
By contrast, AIC showed only a modest association with measured performance (ρ = .46, p < .05).
Importantly, AIC was not itself a domain of self-assessment but rather inferred from behavioral performance
self-assessments and prior knowledge exams can validate internal consistency, but they are insufficient for anticipating who benefits most from AI-mediated learning.

kp.k: Conceptual roadmaps particularly helped low-AIC novices
kp.d: Scaffolded novices scored .45 (SD .14), compared with .38 (SD .22) among unguided LLM novices; the reported difference was weakly significant, .05 < p < .10. The scaffolding–AIC interaction was negative and likewise weakly significant, suggesting greater marginal benefit for low-AIC participants. The authors interpret the lower dispersion as evidence that topic sequencing and conceptual structure can reduce capability-dependent inequalities without lowering average performance.

with a weakly significant difference (p > .05, p < .10).
The coefficient on the interaction term was negative and weakly significant (p > .05, p < .10), indicating that the marginal benefit of scaffolding diminished as AIC increased.
Variance in post-intervention exam scores was lower among scaffolded novices (SD = .14) compared to unguided novices (SD = .22)

kp.k: Additional mandated study time produced no significant improvement
kp.d: Increasing novice study requirements from three to four hours per day produced mean scores of .37 (SD .22), compared with .38 (SD .23) for unguided LLM novices. Controlled OLS models found no significant treatment coefficient. The authors interpret this result as diminishing returns to additional exposure without effective strategies or scaffolding; some participants also reported frustration with the longer requirement.
qs: extending the daily study requirement from three to four hours produced no significant performance gains.
Novices in the “more time” group scored M = .37, SD = .22, statistically indistinguishable from unguided LLM novices, M = .38, SD = .23.
It suggests that simply increasing the quantity of exposure does not reduce inequality when participants lack efficient study strategies.

kp.k: Preference for AI is an imperfect competence indicator
kp.d: Participants preferring LLMs had higher AIC on average (Mann–Whitney p < .05), but preference and competence correlated only r = 0.26. The authors distinguish enthusiastic low-skill users from skilled users preferring other resources. They leave the former group's motivations unresolved and hypothesize that the latter value social learning. The reported logistic regression did not reach conventional significance (p ≈ 0.1), so that explanation remains tentative.
qs: the correlation between preference and ability was only small to moderate (r = 0.26)
Participants with relatively low AIC levels nonetheless expressed a preference for LLMs.
Participants with high AIC levels reported preferring other methods of study.

kp.k: Expandable learning opportunities may create new navigational demands
kp.d: Exploratory analyses suggest learning gains declined more strongly with baseline knowledge under traditional resources than under standard LLM access, notwithstanding the insignificant main treatment–baseline interaction. The authors hypothesize that tailored explanations, follow-ups and examples make AI-assisted learning less bounded. They also suggest that very low-knowledge participants may struggle to exploit this flexibility because they lack the grounding to ask useful questions, recognize misleading answers and consolidate understanding.
qs: Although the formal interaction between treatment and pre-intervention exam score is not statistically significant in our main specification
In the no-LLM condition, gains decline with prior knowledge
By contrast, in the standard LLM condition, this downward relationship is weaker.
A plausible mechanism is that open-ended LLM use creates navigational demands of its own.

kp.k: Authors recommend capability development rather than tool procurement alone
kp.d: The authors recommend diagnosing AIC gaps, training prompting and verification, standardizing workflows, and using feedback to identify failures in human–AI interaction. They extend the learning experiment's mechanisms to analysis, writing and decision support. The discussion asserts that 60–90-minute micro-training and lightweight SOPs can raise the performance floor and reduce variance by about one-third, but the experimental arms described test conceptual scaffolding, additional time and peer collaboration rather than a separate micro-training intervention. These training prescriptions should therefore remain distinguished from the reported roadmap results.
qs: These insights reframe AI adoption as a problem of capability design rather than tool procurement.
Firms can address this gap through targeted micro-training that focuses on prompting logic, verification heuristics, and synthesis structure.
Short interventions of 60–90 minutes can meaningfully raise the performance floor, especially when coupled with light scaffolds such as standardized prompt templates or review checklists.
These process interventions—analogous to standard operating procedures (SOPs) in traditional operations—reduce performance variance by about one-third without diminishing the mean.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Anand and Idan claim that GenAI improves average knowledge-learning performance but distributes gains unevenly according to users’ AI Interaction Competence; structured guidance can narrow these differences.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of education and knowledge work, not legal services. The authors report higher examination performance with LLM-assisted self-study and describe the difference as an approximate 17% productivity lift. They identify AI Interaction Competence (AIC)—prompting, filtering, human verification and iterative application of outputs—as a significant moderator of gains, unlike GPA or prior knowledge. They report that novices benefit especially when AIC is high. Conceptual roadmaps are presented as improving consistency and particularly helping low-AIC novices, whereas an additional mandated study hour produces no significant improvement. The authors also interpret lower attrition in the LLM condition as evidence of greater engagement and perceived resource value. Their broader managerial claim is that AI adoption requires complementary skills and workflow design rather than access alone.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is a randomized student self-study experiment, with examination performance used as a proxy for productivity, alongside subgroup analyses, attrition counts and resource preferences.
pts.d: The working paper reports 179 Texas A&M University participants, predominantly undergraduate engineering students. Participants were randomized between traditional resources and LLM-only study; novices in the latter condition were additionally randomized to standard use, conceptual scaffolding, extra study time or peer collaboration. Post-exam means were 0.56 (SD 0.26) for LLM participants and 0.48 (SD 0.23) for controls; the adjusted treatment coefficient was significant at p < 0.05. GPA and baseline-knowledge interactions were nonsignificant (p = 0.59 and p = 0.2), while the treatment–AIC and three-way treatment–baseline-knowledge–AIC interactions were reported significant at p < 0.05. Scaffolded novices scored 0.45 (SD 0.14), compared with 0.38 (SD 0.22) for unguided novices; both the mean difference and scaffolding–AIC interaction were only weakly significant (0.05 < p < 0.10). Extra-time novices scored 0.37, versus 0.38 for standard LLM novices, without a significant difference. Reported withdrawals numbered 20 in the baseline condition and nine in the LLM condition; 69% preferred LLMs as a learning resource. Analyses used completers. The authors infer motivation from differential attrition, while recording illness and scheduling conflicts as participants’ stated reasons. The discussion recommends 60–90-minute micro-training, but the described randomized interventions do not include a separate micro-training arm. The paper describes AIC measurement inconsistently: the survey section lists self-assessed AIC, whereas the results say it was inferred from behavioral performance rather than self-assessed.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported effects concern a three-day intervention and immediate post-study assessment; wider organizational benefits are conditional managerial extrapolations, not dated long-term forecasts.
pts.d: The supplied working paper is dated 18 May 2026. Participants studied LLMs for three consecutive days, with a minimum of three hours daily, or four hours in the extra-time arm. The LLM condition used only free ChatGPT, with paid subscriptions prohibited; the control condition excluded LLMs. Participants could bring a one-page cheat sheet to the final examination and received completion payments and performance incentives. These are short-horizon learning outcomes, not measurements of sustained workplace productivity. The authors condition equitable gains on effective prompting, interpretation, verification and synthesis, supported by conceptual roadmaps, templates, checklists and training. The described mechanism is human–AI augmentation, not autonomous replacement. No timeframe is specified for broader changes to professional services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is university students; the authors extend the implications to early-career knowledge workers and organizations deploying GenAI.
pts.d: High-AIC users are described as capturing disproportionate gains, including novices with little prior subject knowledge. Low-AIC users may obtain smaller or negative marginal returns and are identified as the principal beneficiaries of conceptual scaffolding. The authors distinguish enthusiasm for LLMs from competence, identifying both enthusiastic but unskilled and skilled but reluctant participants. Managers, onboarding teams and workforce-development functions are urged to diagnose interaction-skill gaps and formalize training and review workflows. The proposed organizational implications cover consulting, finance, analytics, design, engineering, research and professional services. The paper makes no specific finding about lawyers, law firms, legal-service buyers or access to justice, and does not measure employment displacement.
